vo: Look at the sunglasses in your drawer. Maybe they're aviators. Maybe sporty wraparounds. Maybe something expensive with an Italian name.
vis: Slow push-in on a drawer full of different sunglasses under a desk lamp

vo: Different brands. Different prices. Different stores. It feels like choice.
vis: Wall of a sunglass store, dozens of different frames, camera pans

vo: It isn't. There's a good chance most of them came from the same company — a company most people have never even heard of.
vis: Polaroids of different glasses pinned on a board, red strings start connecting them toward one point

vo: It designs the frames. It owns the brands. It owns the stores you buy them in. In America, it even owns one of the insurers that helps pay for them.
vis: Four case-file folders slide onto a desk, one by one: factory, brands, store, insurance card

vo: And when one rival refused to play by its rules, this company didn't just compete. It took that rival off its shelves. Years later, it bought it.
vis: Dark store shelf with empty gaps where products were removed; a red "SOLD" stamp hits a file

vo: This is the story of Luxottica. How an orphan from Milan built one of the most powerful companies you've never heard of — and why your glasses cost what they cost.
vis: Silhouette of a man in a 1950s Milan street, fading into a vast modern factory

vo: Leonardo Del Vecchio was born in Milan in 1935. His father, who sold fruit and vegetables, died when Leonardo was still a baby.
vis: Black-and-white style illustration of a 1930s Milan market stall

vo: When he was seven, his mother couldn't afford to raise him anymore. She handed him over to an orphanage.
vis: A small boy with a suitcase in front of a large old orphanage gate

vo: By fourteen, he was working in a factory. He learned to cut and stamp metal as an apprentice to a tool-and-die maker — tiny parts, including parts for eyeglass frames.
vis: Young worker at an old metal press, sparks, close-up of tiny hinges

vo: In 1961, he moved to Agordo, a small town in the Italian Dolomites, home to much of Italy's eyewear industry. There he opened a workshop. He called it Luxottica.
vis: Mountain village in the Dolomites at dawn, a small workshop with a light on

vo: At first, it made parts for other companies' glasses. But Del Vecchio wanted more. By 1971, Luxottica was selling complete frames under its own name.
vis: Workbench with frame parts, then a finished frame placed in a box

vo: And he had an idea that would shape everything that followed. Why only make the glasses — when you could own every step between the factory and the customer's face?
vis: A map with a red string running from a factory pin to a store pin to a face silhouette

vo: In 1974, he bought his first distributor. In 1981, Luxottica opened its first foreign subsidiary — in Germany.
vis: Vintage delivery truck on an alpine road; a pin on a map of Germany

vo: Then, in 1988, came a deal that changed the industry: Luxottica signed its first licensing deal with a fashion designer, Giorgio Armani.
vis: Elegant 1980s fashion studio, sketches of eyeglass frames on a drafting table

vo: Glasses stopped being a medical device. They became fashion — jewelry for your face. And jewelry can be priced like jewelry.
vis: A pair of glasses displayed like a diamond ring in a glass case, spotlight

vo: Then came the shopping spree. In 1995, Luxottica bought LensCrafters, North America's biggest optical chain.
vis: Polaroid of a large optical store pinned to the board, red string attached

vo: In 1999, it bought Ray-Ban from Bausch & Lomb for 640 million dollars.
vis: Polaroid of classic aviator sunglasses pinned to the board, price tag "$640M" on a file card

vo: At the time, Ray-Ban was in trouble. It had been sold cheaply through thousands of outlets — some pairs for as little as twenty dollars.
vis: Bargain bin full of sunglasses at a gas station counter

vo: Luxottica pulled it out of the bargain bins, fixed the quality and raised the price. Fewer pairs sold — but far more profit.
vis: Same aviators now on a velvet stand in a luxury store, spotlight

vo: In 2001, it bought Sunglass Hut — the biggest sunglass retailer around.
vis: Polaroid of a mall sunglass kiosk pinned to the board

vo: Look at that from a logistics point of view. Luxottica now designed the product, made it, shipped it — and sold it in its own stores.
vis: Animated supply-chain line: factory → container ship → warehouse → store, all marked with the same red pin

vo: Normally, every step in that chain is a different company taking its own margin. Here, every margin landed in the same pocket.
vis: Coins dropping from each step of the chain into one single leather wallet

vo: But owning the stores gave Luxottica something even more valuable than profit: the power to decide which brands customers would see.
vis: A hand rearranging products on a store shelf, some pushed into the shadows

vo: Oakley was the brand that didn't fit. Jim Jannard started it in 1975 in his garage, with 300 dollars.
vis: 1970s California garage with motocross gear and a workbench

vo: It made bold, high-tech sports glasses that athletes loved. By the mid-90s, it was a public company — and a real competitor.
vis: Athlete silhouette with wraparound sport sunglasses, stadium lights

vo: In 1996, Oakley and Luxottica clashed over prices. Luxottica stopped carrying Oakley in its stores. Oakley's stock market value dropped by a third.
vis: Stock chart falling sharply, pinned to the investigation board

vo: Then, in 2001, Luxottica bought Sunglass Hut — one of Oakley's most important shops. Soon after, Oakley products were pushed off its shelves.
vis: Empty shelf section in a sunglass store, dust visible in the light

vo: Oakley fought back. It sued Luxottica, accusing it of selling knockoffs of its designs — and won a court order over its lens technology.
vis: Courtroom scene, gavel, legal documents with redacted lines

vo: By late 2001, the two sides made peace, and Oakley returned to the shelves. But the lesson was obvious. As long as Luxottica owned the stores, Oakley's fate was in Luxottica's hands.
vis: Two chess pieces facing each other, one much larger casting a shadow over the other

vo: In 2007, Luxottica offered 2.1 billion dollars for Oakley. US regulators let the deal through.
vis: Contract on a desk, fountain pen, a red "APPROVED" stamp

vo: The rival that had refused to bend now belonged to the company it had fought.
vis: Oakley-style sport sunglasses polaroid pinned next to the aviators, red string tied between them

vo: But the cleverest part of the machine isn't a brand at all. It might be hidden in your employee benefits.
vis: A benefits card on an office desk, slowly pulled into focus

vo: Luxottica doesn't only make its own brands. It also makes glasses for brands it doesn't own — under license.
vis: Production line with many different frame styles moving past

vo: Chanel. Prada. Armani. Burberry. Versace. Dolce & Gabbana. Michael Kors. Coach. Tiffany. Designed and produced by the same group.
vis: Rapid sequence of elegant luxury eyewear on velvet, each with a red pin

vo: So that wall of "competing" designer brands at the mall? Many of them roll out of the same factories.
vis: Store wall of luxury frames, camera pulls back to reveal one long factory conveyor behind it

vo: In the US, the loop closes even tighter. Luxottica owns EyeMed, one of America's biggest vision insurance companies.
vis: Insurance card pinned on the board, red string leading away from it

vo: Your employer pays for the plan. The plan's network lists stores like LensCrafters, Pearle Vision and Target Optical — stores run by the same group, selling its frames.
vis: Flow diagram on the board: employer → insurance → store → frames, all strings meeting at one pin

vo: To be fair, the network also includes independent eye doctors. But follow the money, and much of it loops back to one place.
vis: Coins travelling along the red string and dropping into one central box

vo: Insurer. Store. Brand. Factory. One company on almost every side of the counter.
vis: Four folders arranged in a circle around a single red pin

vo: In 2012, the TV program 60 Minutes asked Luxottica's then-CEO, Andrea Guerra, why glasses cost so much. His answer: "Everything is worth what people are ready to pay."
vis: Vintage TV set in a dark room showing an interview silhouette

vo: 60 Minutes reported that glasses like these can sell for up to twenty times what they cost to make.
vis: Price tag "×20" hanging from a pair of designer glasses

vo: In 2018, Luxottica merged with Essilor, the French giant behind lenses like Varilux and Crizal. Frames and lenses, under one roof. EssilorLuxottica was worth around 70 billion dollars.
vis: Two company towers (one Italian, one French) connected by a bridge of red string

vo: Leonardo Del Vecchio died in 2022, at 87 — one of the richest people in Europe, worth around 25 billion dollars. The orphan from Milan had built an empire.
vis: Empty office chair at a large desk, a single pair of glasses on the desk, evening light

vo: Today, the group sells through more than 3,000 Sunglass Hut stores, over a thousand LensCrafters, and thousands of other shops around the world.
vis: World map covered in red pins

vo: In 2025, it booked 28.5 billion euros in revenue — a record.
vis: Rising bar chart pinned on the board, warm spotlight

vo: In 2024, it even bought Supreme, the streetwear brand, for 1.5 billion dollars.
vis: Polaroid of a streetwear store in New York pinned to the board

vo: And it has a new partner: Meta. Together they make Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta smart glasses — more than 7 million AI glasses sold in 2025 alone.
vis: Futuristic smart sunglasses with a tiny camera lens, glowing interface reflections

vo: Meta liked the partnership so much that it bought a stake in EssilorLuxottica — worth around three billion euros.
vis: Handshake between a tech silhouette and an eyewear-factory silhouette, documents on the table

vo: Here's the uncomfortable part. Much of what Luxottica did, business schools would admire.
vis: Lecture hall with an empty chalkboard, a single slide of a factory

vo: It rescued brands that were dying. It built factories, stores and logistics that work. Ray-Ban was being sold in bargain bins before Luxottica turned it into an icon again.
vis: Restored vintage aviator sunglasses on a pedestal

vo: But when one company makes the product, owns the store and runs one of the insurers that pays for it, the forces that normally push prices down — competition, comparison, a rival on the next shelf — get a lot weaker.
vis: Scale with one side heavily weighed down by a stack of folders

vo: The choice on the wall is real in one way: different shapes, different logos. But the money behind many of them flows to the same place.
vis: Wall of glasses, the camera follows red strings out of the frame toward one point

vo: And now, as glasses turn into computers with cameras and AI, the company that already sits on millions of faces has teamed up with one of the biggest tech companies on Earth.
vis: A face reflected in smart-glass lenses, data patterns glowing

vo: So the next time you try on a pair at the mall, look past the logo.
vis: Hand picking up sunglasses from a store display

vo: Independent brands and opticians still exist — some sell good frames for a fraction of the price. They're just harder to find, because they aren't on the wall you walk past every day.
vis: Small independent optician's shop on a quiet street, warm light in the window

vo: Ask yourself one question: Am I choosing between brands — or just between price tags of the same company?
vis: The investigation board fully revealed, all strings meeting in the center

vo: Now that you know — would you still pay full price for those sunglasses? Tell me in the comments.
vis: Goldsmith seal (G in magnifying glass) on a dark case file, fade out
